title: A short history of Marvel Comics: Timely, Atlas and Marvel
answer: Marvel began in 1939 as Timely Comics, publisher Martin Goodman's comics line, whose first issue, Marvel Comics #1 (October 1939), introduced the Human Torch and the Sub-Mariner. Through the 1950s the company published as Atlas, mostly genre comics. It became Marvel Comics with the superhero revival led by Stan Lee, Jack Kirby and Steve Ditko from Fantastic Four #1 (November 1961). Marvel was bought by The Walt Disney Company in a deal completed on 31 December 2009.
body:
## Timely (1939–1950)

Goodman, a pulp publisher, entered comics with Marvel Comics #1, produced by the Funnies, Inc. studio: Carl Burgos's Human Torch and Bill Everett's Sub-Mariner. Joe Simon and Jack Kirby's Captain America Comics #1 (March 1941) was the company's wartime hit. Stan Lee, Goodman's relative by marriage, joined in 1939 as an assistant and became editor in 1941. Timely books are the [Golden Age](/collections/golden-age) Marvel keys; see the [Timely Comics publisher page](/publishers/timely-comics).

## Atlas (1950s)

After superheroes faded, the company published Westerns, war, horror, romance, humour and science fiction under the Atlas globe logo (Atlas was Goodman's distribution company). Titles such as Journey into Unknown Worlds, Strange Tales and Journey into Mystery began as Atlas anthologies and later housed the Silver Age debuts. A distribution collapse in 1957 nearly ended the company; it survived on a limited schedule distributed by its rival, DC. See the [Atlas Comics publisher page](/publishers/atlas-comics).

## Marvel (1961–)

Fantastic Four #1 (November 1961) began the run of creations that defines the company: Hulk, Spider-Man and Thor (1962); Iron Man, Doctor Strange, the X-Men and the Avengers (1963); Daredevil (1964); the Silver Surfer, Galactus and Black Panther (1966). Lee's editorial voice, Kirby's design and Ditko's oddness made "the Marvel Age". Every one of those first appearances has a [character page](/characters) on this site.

## Ownership

Goodman sold the company to Perfect Film & Chemical in 1968. It passed through Cadence Industries, New World, and Ronald Perelman's MacAndrews & Forbes, and Marvel Entertainment Group filed for bankruptcy protection in December 1996 after the speculator crash. The company reorganised as Marvel Enterprises, built its film business, and was acquired by Disney in a deal announced in August 2009 and completed on 31 December 2009.

## Distribution

Marvel was distributed exclusively by Diamond from 1995 until it moved to Penguin Random House on 1 October 2021. See [How Marvel and DC changed distribution in 2020–2021](/guides/marvel-dc-distribution-changes-2020-2021).

Browse [Marvel Comics in the store](/publishers/marvel-comics).

title: A short history of DC Comics
answer: DC traces to National Allied Publications, founded by Malcolm Wheeler-Nicholson in 1934, whose New Fun #1 (February 1935) was among the first comics of all-original material. Detective Comics, Inc. (1937) gave the company its initials and, with Action Comics #1 (June 1938), Superman. Sister company All-American Publications added Wonder Woman, the Flash and Green Lantern; the firms merged as National Comics Publications in 1946, became part of Kinney National (later Warner) in 1967, and adopted the name DC Comics officially in 1977.
body:
## Origins

Wheeler-Nicholson's New Fun and More Fun were followed by Detective Comics #1 (March 1937), published by Detective Comics, Inc., a company he formed with Harry Donenfeld and Jack Liebowitz and soon lost to them. Action Comics #1 introduced Superman in 1938 and Detective Comics #27 introduced Batman in 1939 — see [First appearance of Superman](/guides/first-appearance-of-superman) and [First appearance of Batman](/guides/first-appearance-of-batman).

## All-American and the merger

All-American Publications, run by M. C. Gaines and Liebowitz from 1939, published Flash Comics, All-American Comics, All Star Comics and Sensation Comics — the Flash, Green Lantern, Hawkman, the Justice Society and Wonder Woman. Gaines sold out in 1944 and used the money to found EC Comics; the remaining companies merged into National Comics Publications in 1946. The "DC" circle logo appeared on covers from 1940.

## Silver Age and after

Showcase #4 (October 1956) reintroduced the Flash and began the Silver Age. National Periodical Publications (renamed 1961) was bought by Kinney National Company in 1967, which became Warner Communications. The name DC Comics was adopted officially in 1977. Crisis on Infinite Earths (1985–1986) reset the continuity; Watchmen and The Dark Knight Returns (1986) defined the Copper Age; the Vertigo imprint (1993) grew from the Alan Moore Swamp Thing run that produced [John Constantine](/guides/first-appearance-of-john-constantine).

## Recent decades

- **2011** — The New 52 relaunch of the entire line (September 2011); DC leaves the Comics Code.
- **2015** — DC moves from New York to Burbank; Bill Finger credited as Batman's co-creator.
- **2016** — DC Rebirth (May 2016).
- **2020** — DC ends its distribution through Diamond (June 2020) in favour of Lunar Distribution. See [How Marvel and DC changed distribution in 2020–2021](/guides/marvel-dc-distribution-changes-2020-2021).
- **2024** — The Absolute Universe line launches (October 2024).

Browse [DC Comics in the store](/publishers/dc-comics), from Golden Age Superman to Modern Age Batman.

title: EC Comics: the publisher the Comics Code destroyed
answer: EC Comics was founded in 1944 by M. C. Gaines as Educational Comics and turned by his son William Gaines, who took over after his father's death in 1947, into Entertaining Comics: the 1950 “New Trend” horror, crime and science-fiction line, and Mad (1952). Its artists — Wally Wood, Jack Davis, Graham Ingels, Al Williamson, Harvey Kurtzman and others — made it the most admired publisher of the Golden Age. The 1954 Comics Code made its horror and crime titles unpublishable, and by 1956 only Mad, converted to a magazine, remained.
body:
## Two Gaineses

M. C. Gaines, a pioneer of the comic-book format and co-owner of All-American Publications, sold his DC interest in 1944 and founded Educational Comics to publish Picture Stories from the Bible and similar titles. He died in a boating accident in August 1947 and his son William, then a student, inherited a failing company.

## The New Trend

From 1950, William Gaines and editor Al Feldstein relaunched the line as horror (Tales from the Crypt, The Vault of Horror, The Haunt of Fear), crime (Crime SuspenStories, Shock SuspenStories), science fiction (Weird Science, Weird Fantasy) and war (Two-Fisted Tales and Frontline Combat, edited by Harvey Kurtzman). Mad followed in 1952. The stories were literate, ironic and beautifully drawn; the horror hosts and twist endings became the template for the genre.

## The end

EC was the public face of the 1954 campaign against comics. Gaines testified at the Senate subcommittee hearing in April 1954 and was asked whether the Crime SuspenStories #22 cover — a severed head held by the hair — was in good taste. The Comics Code that followed banned everything EC did best. Gaines cancelled the horror and crime titles, tried a short "New Direction" line under the Code, and from 1956 published only Mad, which as a magazine was outside the Code's reach. See [What was the Comics Code Authority?](/guides/what-is-the-comics-code-authority).

## Collecting EC

EC books are collected for artist and story; the Gaines File copies — Gaines's own file copies, sold from the 1980s — are the finest known. See [Collecting EC Comics](/guides/ec-comics-shock-suspenstories-and-panic) and [What is a pedigree comic?](/guides/what-is-a-pedigree-comic). Browse [EC Comics in the store](/publishers/ec-comics).

title: Fawcett Publications and the Marvel Family: a collector's overview
answer: Fawcett Publications, the Minneapolis magazine house behind Captain Billy's Whiz Bang, entered comics in 1940 with Whiz Comics #2 and Captain Marvel, who became the best-selling superhero of the 1940s. Fawcett's line — Whiz Comics, Captain Marvel Adventures, Master Comics, Wow Comics — was ended by a copyright suit from DC that Fawcett settled in 1953. DC later licensed and then acquired the characters, publishing them as Shazam.
body:
## The line

| Title | Years | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Whiz Comics | 1940–1953 | Captain Marvel's home; #2 is the first appearance; #25 first Captain Marvel Jr. |
| Captain Marvel Adventures | 1941–1953 | Solo title; #1 drawn by Jack Kirby; reached bi-weekly at its peak |
| Master Comics | 1940–1953 | Captain Marvel Jr.'s feature from #23 |
| Wow Comics | 1940–1948 | Mary Marvel joined with #9 (January 1943); the Marvel Family's other home |
| Marvel Family | 1945–1954 | Team title |

C. C. Beck's clean art, Otto Binder's scripts and Mac Raboy's Captain Marvel Jr. defined the house style, which was gentler and funnier than DC's or Timely's.

## The lawsuit

National (DC) sued Fawcett in 1941, claiming Captain Marvel infringed Superman. The case ran for over a decade; after an appeals court ruling against Fawcett in 1951 and with superhero sales falling, Fawcett settled in 1953, paid damages and stopped publishing the characters. DC licensed them in 1972, published Shazam! from 1973, and later bought them outright. See [First appearance of Captain Marvel (Shazam)](/guides/first-appearance-of-captain-marvel-shazam).

## Collecting Fawcett

Whiz Comics #2 is a top Golden Age key; Captain Marvel Adventures #1, Whiz Comics #25, Master Comics #21 and Wow Comics #9 are the other major issues. Fawcett printed on decent paper and many books survive in mid grade; high-grade copies are scarce. A [Wow Comics #16 in CGC 9.0 is in the store](/store/wow-comics-16-cgc-9-0). Browse [Fawcett Publications in the store](/publishers/fawcett-publications).

title: MLJ Magazines: the Golden Age superhero publisher that became Archie
answer: MLJ Magazines was founded in 1939 by Maurice Coyne, Louis Silberkleit and John Goldwater (the initials) and published Golden Age superheroes — the Shield in Pep Comics #1 (January 1940), the first patriotic hero, and Steel Sterling in Zip Comics #1 (February 1940). Archie Andrews debuted in Pep Comics #22 (December 1941) and so outsold the heroes that the company renamed itself Archie Comic Publications in 1946.
body:
## The superhero years

MLJ's first title was Blue Ribbon Comics (November 1939). Pep Comics introduced the Shield, a red-white-and-blue hero fourteen months before Captain America. Zip Comics starred Steel Sterling; Top-Notch Comics had the Black Hood and Bob Phantom. The company also published the Hangman and the Wizard, and its covers ran to lurid crime and torture scenes that make certain issues prized by Golden Age collectors.

## Archie

Bob Montana's Archie, introduced as a backup in Pep Comics #22, became the cover feature within a year and had his own title by 1942. By 1946 the humour line dominated and the name changed. The superheroes were revived periodically — as the Mighty Comics line in the 1960s, Red Circle in the 1980s, and Dark Circle in the 2010s.

## Collecting MLJ

- **Pep Comics #1** — first Shield; a major Golden Age key.
- **Pep Comics #22** — first Archie; one of the most valuable Golden Age books outside the superhero genre.
- **Zip Comics** — early issues are scarce; a [Zip Comics #3 in CBCS 3.5 is in the store](/store/zip-comics-3-cbcs-3-5).
- **Pep Comics #17, #36 and other classic covers** — collected for the covers as much as the contents.

Browse [MLJ Magazines in the store](/publishers/mlj-magazines) and the [Golden Age collection](/collections/golden-age).

title: Mirage Studios: the publisher of Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles
answer: Mirage Studios was the name Kevin Eastman and Peter Laird gave the company they formed to self-publish Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles #1 in May 1984 from Dover, New Hampshire — a mirage because there was no studio. The black-and-white comic's success made it the model for the 1980s independent boom, and the licensing that followed built a global franchise. Laird bought out Eastman in 2000 and sold the property to Viacom (Nickelodeon) in 2009.
body:
## The beginning

Eastman and Laird, two young artists sharing a house, drew the Turtles as a joke on Frank Miller's ninja-heavy Daredevil and Ronin, then wrote a 40-page one-shot. They printed about 3,000 copies with a tax refund and a loan from Eastman's uncle, took an ad in the Comic Buyer's Guide, and sold out. The reprints, the issues that followed, and the licensing deal with Playmates Toys (1987) and the animated series (1987) turned a self-published comic into one of the biggest franchises of the decade.

## Mirage as a publisher

Mirage moved to Northampton, Massachusetts, and published the Turtles' main series (volume 1, 1984–1993; volume 2, 1993–1995; volume 4, 2001–2014), spin-offs such as Tales of the TMNT, and creator-owned books by studio members including Stephen Murphy, Jim Lawson and Michael Dooney. The 1990s colour series was published by Archie Comics; IDW has published the Turtles since 2011.

## The black-and-white boom and bust

TMNT #1's success triggered a wave of self-published black-and-white comics in 1985–1987, most of them worthless within a year. The lesson collectors took: a first printing of the real thing (TMNT #1) is scarce and valuable; the imitators printed to meet speculator demand are not.

## Collecting Mirage

See [First appearance of the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles](/guides/first-appearance-of-teenage-mutant-ninja-turtles) and [TMNT #1 printings explained](/guides/tmnt-1-printings-explained). Beyond #1, early first printings of #2–#4 and Raphael #1 (first Casey Jones) are the keys. Browse [Mirage Studios in the store](/publishers/mirage-studios) and the [Copper Age collection](/collections/copper-age).

title: Atlas Comics: Marvel's 1950s horror, fantasy and science-fiction anthologies
answer: Atlas was the name Martin Goodman's comics line used through the 1950s, between Timely and Marvel, after the Atlas News Company that distributed it. It published dozens of genre anthologies — Journey into Unknown Worlds, Strange Tales, Journey into Mystery, Adventures into Terror, Menace, Uncanny Tales — with art by Bill Everett, Joe Maneely, Russ Heath, Gene Colan, John Romita and Jack Kirby. Pre-Code Atlas horror is collected in its own right, and several Atlas anthologies later housed the Silver Age Marvel debuts.
body:
## The anthologies

| Title | Years | Later significance |
|---|---|---|
| Journey into Unknown Worlds | 1950–1957 | Pre-Code science fiction and horror; began by continuing Teen Comics' numbering (#36–38), then restarted at #4 in 1951 |
| Strange Tales | 1951–1968 | Later the home of the Human Torch, Doctor Strange (#110) and Nick Fury (#135) |
| Journey into Mystery | 1952–1966 | Later the home of Thor (#83) |
| Menace | 1953–1954 | Pre-Code horror; #1 has Everett, Heath and Maneely art |
| Tales to Astonish, Tales of Suspense | 1959– | Started as monster books at the very end of the Atlas era; later Ant-Man, Hulk, Iron Man and Captain America |

## Pre-Code Atlas horror

Before the 1954 Code, Atlas published more horror titles than any other company. The best issues — with Everett, Maneely and Heath covers — are valued alongside EC and Harvey pre-Code horror, though Atlas stories are generally less celebrated than EC's. A [Journey into Unknown Worlds #10 (1952) in CGC 8.0 is in the store](/store/journey-into-unknown-worlds-10-cgc-8-0).

## The 1957 collapse

Goodman closed Atlas News in late 1956 and moved to American News Company, which collapsed within months. Goodman was forced into a distribution deal with Independent News — owned by DC — that limited him to eight titles a month for years. The company that survived that squeeze was the one Lee and Kirby rebuilt from 1961.

## Dating an Atlas book

The Atlas globe logo appeared on covers from late 1951 to 1957; the Comics Code seal appears from 1955. The indicia names one of many Goodman shell companies rather than "Atlas".

See [A short history of Marvel Comics](/guides/history-of-marvel-comics) and browse [Atlas Comics in the store](/publishers/atlas-comics).

title: Timely Comics: collecting Golden Age Marvel
answer: Timely Comics was Martin Goodman's comics line from Marvel Comics #1 (October 1939) through the 1940s — the Golden Age incarnation of Marvel. Its big three were the Human Torch, the Sub-Mariner and Captain America, and its keys — Marvel Comics #1, Captain America Comics #1, Marvel Mystery Comics, Human Torch #2 (#1), All Winners Comics — are among the most valuable Golden Age books. A CGC 9.4 Marvel Comics #1 sold for 2.4 million dollars in March 2022.
body:
## The titles

- **Marvel Comics #1** (October 1939), retitled **Marvel Mystery Comics** from #2 — the flagship anthology with the Human Torch and Sub-Mariner; their fight across #8–10 (1940) is the first superhero crossover. A [Marvel Mystery Comics #19 (May 1941) is in the store](/store/marvel-mystery-comics-19-cbcs-7-0).
- **Captain America Comics** (1941–1950) — Simon and Kirby's hero; see [First appearance of Captain America](/guides/first-appearance-of-captain-america).
- **Human Torch** (1940–1954), **Sub-Mariner Comics** (1941–1955), **All Winners Comics** (1941–1947, the All-Winners Squad in #19 and #21), **Young Allies**, **USA Comics**, **Daring Mystery**, **Mystic Comics**.

## The people

Joe Simon was the first editor; Stan Lee succeeded him in 1941 at nineteen and remained, with wartime service, until 1972. Artists included Jack Kirby, Bill Everett, Carl Burgos, Alex Schomburg (whose busy war covers are the most collected Timely covers), Syd Shores and Al Avison.

## Collecting Timely

Timely paper and printing were poor, wartime paper drives consumed most copies, and survival is low; mid-grade copies of the major titles are scarce and high grades are exceptional. Schomburg covers, Japanese and Nazi war covers, and the early Torch–Namor issues carry premiums. Restoration is common — buy graded.

See [A short history of Marvel Comics](/guides/history-of-marvel-comics) and browse [Timely Comics in the store](/publishers/timely-comics) and the [Golden Age collection](/collections/golden-age).
